About.AboutText:
Hi, I am Jayden Kalberer. I am a passionate Electrical Engineering student with a keen interest in PCB design and power systems. Currently, I am pursuing my undergraduate degree at Seattle Pacific University. I am dedicated to expanding my knowledge and skills in various areas of Electrical Engineering.

I enjoy tackling challenging engineering projects and I thrive in collaborative environments where I can contribute my expertise and learn from my peers.

I am professionally interested in fields relating to aviation, automotive, or robotics. Growing up in a family filled with airplane and automotive mechanics instilled a lifelong passion. My interest in robotics started after taking a related course in high school. To be a part of the design process relating to one of these fields would be a dream come true.

Project1.Title: Gravity Lamp
Project1.Desc:
The Gravity Lamp is a project I made with three other engineering students for my Junior Design class at SPU. The goal was to create a portable light that could be recharged by converting gravitational energy into electricity. I was in charge of developing the Power Generation and Storage subsystem (See More Slide 1) and the Lighting subsystem. This involved sourcing and testing our generator under a simulated load to find the optimal RPM the generator needs to spin at to produce the required voltage and amperage to charge our chosen battery (See More Slide 2). As for the Lighting subsystem, I designed a lighting circuit that would produce at least 400 lumens of light when powered along with our other electrical components (See More Slide 3).

Here is a link to a video going over the full project: https://youtu.be/6dhxcbBb5b4?si=gkZMMuPDTXkZDUjW.

Project2.Title: DC Power Supply
Project2.Desc: This circuit is a DC power supply offering multiple output levels that I made myself for my Electronics 1 class at SPU (See More Slide 1). It is powered by a 10:1 center-tapped step-down transformer connected to a standard 120 V AC wall outlet. The output terminals provide three fixed voltage levels, three adjustable voltage levels, and a ground connection. The transformer delivers a 12 V AC input, which is rectified by a diode bridge to produce positive and negative outputs. These outputs feed five voltage regulators. An operational amplifier, powered by the +12 V and –12 V voltage regulators, supplies an isolated output. Potentiometers are used to adjust the output voltages of the two adjustable regulators and the op-amp. I used Altium and LTspice to develop and create the PCB for this circuit (See More Slides 1-3).

Project3.Title: 4th Order Sallen-Key Bandpass Filter at 25kHz
Project3.Desc:
My filter consisted of two stages; the first stage has a Q value of 3.5, and the second stage has a Q value of 4.0. For the first stage, the gain was 1.96 V/V dB, and for the second stage, the gain was 2.2 V/V. This results in the filter having a total gain of 4.28 V/V at 25 kHz. It also included a built-in peak detector and comparator that turns on an LED to show that the correct frequency is coming from the input signal. To develop this circuit, I primarily used LTspice.
